summary: A structure in C is a user-defined data type that groups variables of different data types under a single name, making it easier to manage related data.
shortNotes: A structure is declared using the `struct` keyword followed by a tag name and member list inside curly braces.
Members of a structure can be of different data types such as int, float, char, or even other structures.
Structure variables are accessed using the dot operator (.) for normal variables and arrow operator (->) for pointers.
Memory is allocated for all members of a structure; the total size is at least the sum of sizes of all members (may be more due to padding).
Structures can be passed to functions either by value (a copy is made) or by reference (using a pointer).
The `typedef` keyword can be used with structures to create a shorter alias, avoiding repeated use of the `struct` keyword.

detailed.explanation:
A **structure** in C lets you group together variables of different types under one name. For example, a student has a name (string), roll number (int), and marks (float). Instead of keeping three separate variables, you can bundle them into a single `struct Student`. This keeps your code organized and logical.

You define a structure using the `struct` keyword, a tag name, and a list of **members** inside curly braces, ending with a semicolon. Once defined, you can create variables of that structure type just like you create `int` or `float` variables. For example: `struct Student s1;` creates a variable `s1` of type `struct Student`.

To access the members of a structure variable, you use the **dot operator** (`.`). For example, `s1.rollNo = 10;` sets the roll number. If you have a pointer to a structure, you use the **arrow operator** (`->`) instead: `ptr->rollNo = 10;`. Both do the same job but apply in different situations.

Structures can be **nested**, meaning a structure can contain another structure as a member. They can also be used inside arrays — an array of structures is very useful when handling records of multiple students, employees, or products. You can also pass structures to functions, either by value or by pointer.

Using `typedef` with structures is a popular shortcut. Instead of writing `struct Student s1;` every time, you can define `typedef struct { int rollNo; float marks; } Student;` and then simply write `Student s1;`. This makes the code cleaner and easier to read.

definitions.meaning: A user-defined data type in C that groups variables of different types under a single name using the `struct` keyword.
An individual variable declared inside a structure, which can be of any valid C data type.
The operator used to access a member of a structure variable directly, e.g., `s1.rollNo`.
The operator used to access a member of a structure through a pointer, e.g., `ptr->rollNo`.
A keyword used to create an alias for an existing data type, often used with structures to avoid writing `struct` repeatedly.
A structure that contains another structure as one of its members.
Extra bytes added by the compiler between structure members to align data in memory for faster access.

points: The `struct` keyword is mandatory when declaring a structure type and its variables (unless `typedef` is used).
All members of a structure are stored in contiguous memory locations, but padding may increase the total size.
Use `sizeof(struct TagName)` to find the memory occupied by a structure — this is a common exam question.
The dot operator (`.`) is used with structure variables; the arrow operator (`->`) is used with structure pointers.
Structures cannot have functions as members in C (unlike C++ classes), only data members.
An array of structures is declared as: `struct Student arr[50];` — useful for storing multiple records.
When a structure is passed to a function by value, changes inside the function do NOT affect the original; use pointers to modify the original.
Structures can be initialized at the time of declaration: `struct Student s1 = {1, "Rahul", 85.5};`

commonMistakes: Using `=` to copy a string into a char array member (e.g., `s1.name = "Rahul";`) — this is invalid in C; always use `strcpy(s1.name, "Rahul");` instead.
Using the dot operator (`.`) with a pointer to a structure instead of the arrow operator (`->`), e.g., writing `ptr.rollNo` when `ptr` is a pointer — the correct form is `ptr->rollNo`.
Forgetting the semicolon at the end of the structure definition — `struct Student { ... };` must end with `;`, otherwise the compiler throws an error.

questions.prompt: Which keyword is used to define a structure in C?
questions.explanation: The `struct` keyword is used to define a structure in C. `union` is a different user-defined type, `typedef` creates aliases, and `record` is not a C keyword.

questions.prompt: Which operator is used to access a member of a structure through a pointer?
questions.explanation: The arrow operator `->` is used to access structure members via a pointer. The dot operator `.` is used with normal structure variables.

questions.prompt: What will `sizeof(struct Point)` return for `struct Point { int x; int y; };` on a system where int is 4 bytes?
questions.explanation: The structure has two int members, each 4 bytes, so the total size is 4 + 4 = 8 bytes (assuming no extra padding between two ints of same size).

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly initializes a structure variable at the time of declaration?
questions.explanation: Structures are initialized using `=` followed by values in curly braces in the same order as the members are declared. The tag name must be used after `struct`.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of `typedef` when used with a structure?
options: It allocates memory for the structure automatically
It creates an alias so you can use the structure without writing `struct` each time
It allows the structure to have function members
questions.explanation: `typedef` creates a new name (alias) for the structure type. For example, `typedef struct { int x; } Point;` lets you write `Point p;` instead of `struct Point p;`.

questions.prompt: When a structure is passed to a function by value, what happens to the original structure if the function modifies it?
options: The original structure is also modified
The structure is deleted after the function returns
questions.explanation: Passing by value creates a copy of the structure inside the function. Any changes made to the copy do not affect the original variable in the calling function.

questions.prompt: What is a nested structure in C? Give a brief example.
questions.answer: A nested structure is a structure that contains another structure as one of its members. For example, a `struct Date` can be a member inside `struct Employee`, so each employee record stores a date of joining as a structure.
questions.explanation: Nesting lets you model real-world hierarchies. For example, an address (street, city, pin) can be a sub-structure inside an Employee structure, keeping related data grouped together.

questions.prompt: Why can't you use the assignment operator (=) to copy a string into a char array member of a structure? What should you use instead?
questions.answer: In C, arrays cannot be assigned using `=` after declaration; it only works for single characters or at initialization. For copying strings into char array members, you must use `strcpy()` from the `string.h` library.
questions.explanation: In C, an array name is a constant pointer, so you cannot reassign it. The `strcpy` function copies characters one by one from the source string to the destination array.

questions.prompt: Consider: struct Box { char a; int b; char c; }; On a system where char is 1 byte and int is 4 bytes, and the compiler aligns int on a 4-byte boundary, what is the output of printf("%lu", sizeof(struct Box)); ?
questions.explanation: With padding: `a` takes 1 byte + 3 bytes padding = 4 bytes; `b` takes 4 bytes; `c` takes 1 byte + 3 bytes padding = 4 bytes. Total = 12 bytes. This is a classic structure padding example.

questions.prompt: Write a C program that defines a structure `Rectangle` with two float members `length` and `width`. In main, create a structure variable, read length and width from the user, and print the area and perimeter of the rectangle.
questions.explanation: First, define `struct Rectangle` with `length` and `width` as float members. In `main`, declare a variable `r` of this type. Use `scanf` with `&r.length` and `&r.width` to read values. Calculate area as length times width, and perimeter as 2 times the sum of length and width. Print both using `printf` with `%.2f` format for two decimal places.

steps.say: Hello everyone! Today we are going to learn about Structures in C. Structures are one of the most useful tools in C programming.
Imagine you want to store information about a student. A student has a roll number, a name, and marks. These are three different types of data.
Instead of creating three separate variables, a structure lets you bundle all of them under one name. That is the whole idea behind a structure.

write.content:
Group different data types
under ONE name

steps.say: Let us see how to write a structure in C. We use the struct keyword, then give it a name, and list the members inside curly braces.
Inside the structure, we list the members. Here we have roll number as int, name as a char array, and marks as float.
We close the curly brace and put a semicolon at the end. This semicolon is very important and a common place to make mistakes.
Now to create a variable of this type, we write struct Student and then the variable name. This creates a variable s1 in memory.

scenes.title: Accessing Members using Dot and Arrow Operators

steps.say: To put values into the members of a structure variable, we use the dot operator. Write the variable name, then a dot, then the member name.
For the name member, we cannot use equals directly because name is a char array. We must use the strcpy function.
Now if we have a pointer to the structure, we use the arrow operator instead of the dot. These two lines do exactly the same thing.
Remember this rule: dot for normal variables, arrow for pointers. This comes up in almost every exam on structures.

write.content:
Variable  ->  use dot (.)
Pointer   ->  use arrow (->)

steps.say: You can create an array of structures to store records for many students. Here we create an array for 50 students.
Access each student using the index and dot operator. For example, class of index zero dot rollNo gives the roll number of the first student.
Using typedef, we can give the structure a shorter alias. After this, we can write Student directly without the struct keyword every time.
Let us quickly recap what we learned today. A structure groups different data types under one name using the struct keyword.
We use the dot operator to access members of a normal structure variable, and the arrow operator for pointers.

write.content:
dot (.) for variable
arrow (->) for pointer

steps.say: Always end the structure definition with a semicolon, and use strcpy for copying strings into char array members.

write.content:
End struct with ;
Use strcpy for strings

steps.say: Structures make your programs cleaner and easier to manage, especially when dealing with real-world records like students or employees. Great work today!
